sentences.text: Agustinia is a genus of sauropod dinosaur that contains only one known species, Agustinia ligabuei.
The animal is known solely from broken remains, such as vertebrae from the back, hips, and tail.
Broken pieces of the lower hind leg, including a fibula and tibia, were also found.
One of the recovered fibula bones measures approximately 895 mm in length.
Based on this bone size, scientists estimate the creature reached a total length of about 15 meters.
A single fibula bone found in the fossil record measures exactly 895 mm long.
Comparison with related dinosaurs suggests this sauropod may have grown to be 15 meters long.
The genus name honors Agustín Martinelli, the student who found the skeleton during an excavation.
Jose Bonaparte first described the animal in 1999, a work that also introduced the family name Agustiniidae.
The specific name ligabuei was chosen to honor Dr. Giancarlo Ligabue, a philanthropist who funded the expedition.

The holotype specimen, kept at the Municipal Museum Carmen Funes in Plaza Huincul, includes three incomplete dorsal vertebrae, six sacral vertebrae, ten caudal vertebrae, nine pieces considered osteoderms, most of the right tibia and ulna, and five articulated left metatarsals.
Agustinia was a four-legged plant eater like other known sauropods.
Other dinosaurs, including the rebbachisaurid Comahuesaurus and the somphospondylid Ligabuesaurus, have been named from the same formation.
Initially, Agustinia was thought to possess a body armor with a series of broad, vertical points and plates on its back, leading Bonaparte to propose the new family Agustiniidae.
Later studies of poorly preserved fossil material showed that the bony plates were very likely fragments of rib and hip bones.
Bonaparte noted that the four perpendicular laminae with the postspinal laminae are most similar to rebbachisaurids rather than titanosaurians, and the parent group of Agustinia is Rebbachisauridae.
D'emic et al. concluded there were no diagnostic features to classify Agustinia within Diplodocoidea or Titanosauria, so they classified it as incertae sedis.
Agustinia lived approximately 116 to 108 million years ago during the Early Cretaceous Period, specifically from 113.2 to 100.5 million years ago during the Albian stage.
Agustinia fossils were found in the Lohan Cura Formation of the Early Cretaceous in Neuquén Province, Argentina.
Some authors consider Agustinia a nomen dubium due to its fragmentary nature and lack of distinctive characteristics.

It is debated whether Agustinia is a diplodocoid or titanosaurian based on conflicting vertebral features, as diplodocoids have compressed dorsal spines while titanosaurians have six sacral vertebrae.
